title: 7 Geopolitical Scenarios — Hormuz, TurkStream, and the EU LNG Ban
hook: The Strait of Hormuz remains closed to commercial traffic for a 39th day, while US-Iran ceasefire talks in Islamabad hang in the balance. With TurkStream still flowing and the EU's Russian LNG spot ban looming April 25, the gas market is caught between escalation fatigue and structural supply risks.
authorWord: Apex's 7-scenario framework is solid. The most probable path (statu quo with prolonged ceasefire) prices in TTF 40-50, but the tail risks on both sides remain elevated. Keep risk limits tight.
author: La Rédaction 🦊
details:
🔥 BULL EXTRÊME — Islamabad Talks Collapse (10% prob): The April 11 Islamabad round between Vice President Vance and Iranian officials (Araghchi, Ghalibaf) ends without agreement. Trump resumes threats to destroy Iranian bridges and gas infrastructure. The IRGC's destruction of a US drone on April 11 escalates into direct naval engagement. The 2-week ceasefire (expiring ~April 22) unravels. Hormuz becomes completely inaccessible, and Qatar cannot export via the strait. TTF spikes to €75-100/MWh (Goldman Sachs projection). Q2-Q3 contracts rally massively, and 2027+ LT contracts hit multi-year highs.

💣 HIGH RISK — Naval Incident in Hormuz Mine-Clearing (15% prob): Two US destroyers entered Hormuz on April 11 to begin mine-clearing operations. The IRGC has promised 'severe response' to any military passage. An accidental or deliberate exchange of fire between US Navy and IRGC boats during mine-clearing is plausible in the next 2 weeks. Commercial tankers immediately withdraw, risk premium on LNG freight explodes (+$2-3/MMBtu). TTF jumps €15-25/MWh in a single session. Any hope of Hormuz reopening is delayed by weeks.

🔄 BASE CASE — Statuquo Tendu: Ceasefire Prolongé Sans Réouverture (30% prob): Pakistan (Munir, Dar) pushes to extend the ceasefire beyond April 22 despite the failed first round. Iran maintains the strait 'effectively closed' with tolls exceeding $1M per vessel (NYT, April 9). No meaningful mutual concessions. US/CENTCOM mine-clearing progresses slowly. The market gradually prices in the 'new normal': TTF stabilizes at €40-50/MWh but with elevated volatility. Qatar's force majeure continues (The National: restart not before late August). 12-14% of EU LNG (Qatar volumes) remains offline.

🏛️ REGULATORY SHOCK — EU Spot Russian LNG Ban April 25 (20% prob): The EU's 13th sanctions package, adopted March 2026, bans spot Russian LNG imports by April 25. Long-term contracts (~10-12 bcm/yr to Spain, Belgium, France, Greece) are exempt, but spot volumes had grown in Q1 2026 as EU members 'quietly ramped up' purchases (FT, April 10) ahead of the ban. Immediate removal of ~15-20 bcm/yr of spot Russian LNG from the EU market. Short-term impact moderate (storage at 29% in April), but TTF pressure +€5-10/MWh if combined with extended Hormuz closure. Q3 seasonal premium widens.

⚓ MODERATE BULL — Partial Hormuz Reopening Under IRGC Coordination (15% prob): Iran accepts a 'technical' limited reopening with IRGC coordination and high tolls, as the Iranian foreign minister hinted on April 9 ('safe passage under technical limitations'). US/CENTCOM mine-clearing advances. QatarEnergy prepares a partial restart of operational Ras Laffan trains (Reuters, April 8). Gradual return of 50-100 mcm/d of Qatari LNG to Asia/EU (out of ~300 mcm/d normal). Ras Laffan trains 4 and 6 remain damaged (17% of export capacity lost for years). TTF declines €5-10/MWh. Market stabilizes.

⚓ MILD BULL — TurkStream Stability + Asian LNG Rediversion to EU (5% prob): TurkStream continues delivering ~15 bcm/yr to Hungary, Serbia, and Austria (flows confirmed stable). With the EU spot Russian LNG ban taking effect April 25, Central European countries rely more heavily on TurkStream for supply security. Meanwhile, US and African LNG cargoes are redirected from Asia to Europe, partially offsetting Qatar's reduced volumes. Net effect neutral to slightly bearish for TTF (-€2-3/MWh). TurkStream's strategic value to Central Europe increases, potentially shielding it from future sanctions.

🔻 BEAR EXTRÊME — Ceasefire Extended + Full Hormuz Reopening + Mild Weather (5% prob): Islamabad talks surprise with a framework agreement. A 60-day ceasefire extension is announced. Iran accepts full Hormuz reopening under international monitoring. Mine-clearing completes rapidly. QatarEnergy announces accelerated restart of damaged Ras Laffan trains by July. Simultaneously, Europe experiences a mild April-May, reducing demand. The combined supply positive and demand negative crush TTF to €25-30/MWh. The market reverses entirely, with bearish sentiment dominating heading into summer.

💡 Trade Ideas

1. Long June TTF €50 Calls (Asymmetric Upside): With 55% combined probability assigned to the two extreme bull scenarios (collapse, naval incident), plus 20% for the EU ban shock, the upside skew is significant. Buying June €50 calls at €0.8-1.0 offers limited downside (premium paid) with leveraged exposure to any escalation. Maximum loss = premium. Profit potential 5-10x on Hormuz-related headlines.

2. Short June TTF €35 Puts (Fade the Bear Case): The extreme bear scenario (Hormuz reopening + mild weather) is assigned only 5% probability. Selling June €35 puts at €0.6-0.8 captures premium with low probability of assignment. Requires margin management. Stop if TTF breaks €40 on heavy volume.

3. Calendar Spread — Buy Dec 2026 / Sell Jun 2026 (Structural Bull): Even if near-term volatility eases, structural supply risks (Hormuz, EU ban, TurkStream dependence) support winter 2026/27 contracts. Buying December 2026 TTF and selling June 2026 captures the seasonal and risk premium buildup. Target spread widening from current €5 to €12-15 by November.

⚡ Dissenting View — Dante 🔥
You're underestimating the coordination risk. A single false move — one IRGC boat gets too close to a US minesweeper, one drone strays into restricted airspace — and we're in Scenario 2. The tail isn't 10% collapse, it's 40% chaos. The base case should be 'indefinite closure until November,' not 'prolonged ceasefire.' Your probabilities are too complacent.
